The bulk tank was topped up just before the decline, and the delivery slip shows a smaller volume than the tank level rise suggests.
Raw-water turbidity, pH, and alkalinity are steady, and the feed pump output was verified by a drawdown test.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The feed pump is under-delivering against its setting
Raw-water coagulant demand has risen
The alum in the plant tank is diluted, so the set dose delivers less active coagulant than intended
The flocculator paddles have slowed down

inference.explanation: Fresh alum works at the normal dose, day tank alum needs double, its density is low, and the pump passed a drawdown test. That is diluted chemical in the tank. Pump delivery and raw demand are cleared by the drawdown test and steady raw quality, and paddle speed is not implicated by any observation.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms dilution at delivery?

options.label: Archived flocculator speed log
Archived delivery records and tank level readings around the refill
Archived raw-water jar test results from last season

nextClue.explanation: Archived delivery records and tank level readings around the refill directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Flocculator speed was steady, which does not explain weak jar results using day tank chemical.
clueText.nc-b: Records show the tank rose by about 9000 L on a 5000 L delivery, indicating roughly 4000 L of other liquid, consistent with the low density reading.
clueText.nc-c: Last season the jar tests were normal, which only dates the problem to the recent refill.

tasks.prompt: A chlorine gas detector alarms repeatedly in the afternoon, but leak checks at every chlorine joint are negative.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A second, portable detector carried through the room reads normal at all chlorine equipment.
Ammonia leak checks at the cylinder, regulator, and chlorinator joints show no fumes anywhere.
The fixed detector alarms begin each time a strong solvent cleaner is used on the floor near its sensor, noted in the cleaning log.
Moving a test exposure of the cleaner vapour near the sensor in a controlled trial triggers the same alarm.
Chlorine feed, residuals, and cylinder weights are all normal, and no chlorine odour is present.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The fixed detector is cross-sensitive to the solvent cleaner vapour and is giving false alarms
There is a real chlorine leak too small for the ammonia test
The portable detector is faulty and missing a real leak
Chlorine is leaking only in the afternoons when feed is highest

inference.explanation: Alarms track solvent use, a controlled solvent exposure triggers the alarm, and every leak check plus a portable detector are negative. That is cross-sensitivity. A real leak would be expected to show on at least one independent check, the portable unit verified normally on test gas in the trial notes, and feed rates do not follow the cleaning schedule.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the cross-sensitivity pattern?

options.label: Archived chlorine leak check records
Archived detector alarm history paired with the room cleaning log
Archived portable detector calibration log

nextClue.explanation: Archived detector alarm history paired with the room cleaning log directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Leak checks throughout that period were all negative.
clueText.nc-b: Alarm timestamps line up with solvent cleaning sessions across six weeks, and never with cylinder changes or feed changes.
clueText.nc-c: Portable detector calibrations and bump tests have passed.

tasks.prompt: A clarifier with a theoretical detention time of about 3 hours shows floc at the effluent weir far sooner than expected after startup.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Dye added at the inlet appears at the effluent weir in about 20 minutes.
Most of the basin surface is calm, with a visible fast stream running from inlet to outlet along one side.
The inlet baffle was found tilted and partly detached during a basin inspection last week.
Settled turbidity is poor even though floc entering the basin is large and settles well in a cylinder test.
Flow, dose, and sludge blanket depth are all in their normal ranges.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge blanket has risen and is washing over the weir
The coagulant dose is too low to form settleable floc
The basin is hydraulically overloaded beyond its design flow
Water is short-circuiting through the basin because the damaged inlet baffle lets a jet stream straight to the outlet

inference.explanation: Dye crosses in 20 minutes against a 3 hour theoretical time, a fast side stream is visible, the inlet baffle is damaged, and floc settles well in a cylinder. That is short-circuiting. Blanket, dose, and flow are all recorded as normal or proven good by the cylinder test.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the short-circuit path?

options.label: Archived sludge blanket survey
Archived plant flow records
Archived dye tracer study results for this basin

nextClue.explanation: Archived dye tracer study results for this basin directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The blanket survey shows a normal, even blanket, which clears sludge washout.
clueText.nc-b: Flow records confirm operation within design flow all week.
clueText.nc-c: The tracer study shows a sharp early peak at 18 minutes and a long tail, the classic short-circuit pattern for this basin.

tasks.prompt: Settled-water turbidity rose through the week and solids are now visible rolling over the clarifier weir, especially late in each day.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Sludge blanket depth measures 1.3 m, up from a normal 0.3 m, and is deepest near the outlet end.
The sludge withdrawal pump was found valved out for maintenance five days ago and never returned to service.
Settled samples are worst in the afternoon, when the warmed surface layer is most disturbed.
Floc entering the basin is normal in size and settles well in a cylinder test.
Plant flow and coagulant dose are unchanged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge blanket has built up because sludge withdrawal has been out of service, and solids are washing out
The coagulant dose is too low for the raw water
The inlet baffle has failed and the basin is short-circuiting
Raw-water turbidity has spiked beyond the clarifier capacity

inference.explanation: The blanket is four times its normal depth, the withdrawal pump has been valved out for five days, and entering floc settles well in a cylinder. That is blanket buildup from no sludge removal. Dose is proven by the cylinder test, and no baffle or raw spike observation is present.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the withdrawal outage timeline?

options.label: Archived sludge pump run log and valve maintenance record
Archived jar test log
Archived raw-water turbidity trend

nextClue.explanation: Archived sludge pump run log and valve maintenance record directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The log shows zero sludge pump run hours for five days, matching the maintenance record that valved it out and never signed it back in.
clueText.nc-b: Jar tests were normal all week, which clears coagulant dose.
clueText.nc-c: Raw turbidity stayed in its usual band, which clears a raw-water spike.

tasks.prompt: Clarifier performance fell sharply during a wet-weather day even though chemical treatment looks correct.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Plant flow rose from 90 L/s to 175 L/s over three hours as storm runoff entered the source.
The surface overflow rate is now roughly double the rate the clarifier normally runs at.
Floc is well formed and settles quickly in a cylinder test, leaving clear water above.
The sludge blanket is at normal depth and sludge withdrawal is running.
Settled turbidity improves noticeably during a brief period when flow eases back toward 120 L/s.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The coagulant dose is too low for the raw water
The clarifier is hydraulically overloaded, so floc does not have enough settling time or area
The sludge blanket has built up and is washing out
The flocculator is shearing the floc before settling

inference.explanation: Flow and overflow rate doubled, floc settles well in a cylinder, the blanket is normal, and performance recovers when flow eases. That is hydraulic overload. Dose and shear are disproven by the cylinder test, and the blanket measurement clears washout.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the overload threshold for this basin?

options.label: Archived sludge pump run log
Archived settled turbidity versus plant flow records from past wet-weather events
Archived alum dose log

nextClue.explanation: Archived settled turbidity versus plant flow records from past wet-weather events directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The sludge pump ran normally, which matches the normal blanket depth.
clueText.nc-b: Past events show settled turbidity climbing whenever flow passes about 140 L/s, and today the plant ran at 175 L/s for hours.
clueText.nc-c: The dose log shows the dose was raised with flow as intended.

tasks.prompt: Sludge is accumulating in a deep cone at the centre of a circular clarifier, and settled quality is slowly worsening.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The sludge rake drive shows a high-torque alarm history and the rake arm does not move when observed.
Sludge sampled at the centre is old, dark, and releases gas bubbles when disturbed.
Blanket depth is very uneven, deep at the centre and thin near the walls.
Sludge withdrawal from the centre hopper draws mostly thin, watery sludge despite the deep centre blanket.
Influent floc quality and plant flow are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge withdrawal pump has lost capacity
The coagulant dose is producing too much sludge for the basin
The sludge rake has stopped, so sludge is not being moved to the withdrawal hopper
The clarifier is short-circuiting along one wall

inference.explanation: The rake does not move, torque alarms are logged, the blanket is deep at the centre and thin at the walls, and centre sludge is old and gassy. That is a stopped rake. A weak pump would not leave the blanket pattern uneven, dose affects both zones equally, and short-circuiting would show a flow path rather than a centre cone.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the rake stoppage?

options.label: Archived sludge pump capacity test
Archived dye tracer study
Archived rake drive torque and run status trend

nextClue.explanation: Archived rake drive torque and run status trend directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The pump capacity test was satisfactory last month, and the pump draws what reaches the hopper.
clueText.nc-b: The tracer study from commissioning showed even flow distribution, not a centre sludge cone.
clueText.nc-c: The trend shows torque spiking to the trip point six days ago, with no run time since, matching the age of the centre sludge.

tasks.prompt: One side of a rectangular clarifier produces noticeably cloudier water over its weir than the other side.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A thick mat of green algae and slime coats the effluent launder and weir plates on the cloudy side only.
Water depth over the weir plate is uneven, with visibly more flow spilling at the slime-coated sections.
The clean side of the same basin produces settled water at 1.1 NTU, and the cloudy side measures 2.9 NTU.
Floc quality, dose, flow, and blanket depth are normal and even across the basin.
The launder on the cloudy side was last cleaned eight months ago, and the clean side was cleaned last month.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The basin is short-circuiting from inlet to outlet
The sludge blanket has risen on one side of the basin
The coagulant dose is too low on one side of the basin
Algae and slime growth on the weir has made flow over the weir uneven and is sloughing solids into the effluent

inference.explanation: Growth is heavy on the cloudy side only, flow over that weir is uneven, the other side of the same basin is clear, and cleaning history differs by side. That points to the fouled weir. Dose is common to the whole basin, the blanket is even, and a short circuit would not follow the launder cleaning pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the weir growth effect?

options.label: Archived launder cleaning records paired with side-by-side settled turbidity samples
Archived inlet flow distribution study
Archived alum dose log

nextClue.explanation: Archived launder cleaning records paired with side-by-side settled turbidity samples directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Past records show the same side-by-side turbidity gap whenever that launder went more than six months between cleanings, closing after each cleaning.
clueText.nc-b: The flow study showed even inlet distribution, which argues against a one-sided flow path.
clueText.nc-c: The dose log is a single common feed and cannot differ by side.

tasks.prompt: A Saskatchewan clarifier loses settled-water quality every cold snap, with floc appearing at the weir soon after the basin ices over.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: A continuous ice sheet covers about 70 percent of the basin surface.
Open water is confined to a channel between the inlet and the effluent launder.
Dye added at the inlet reaches the weir in about 25 minutes, against a theoretical detention time near 3 hours.
Floc settles well in an indoor cylinder test at the same dose.
Plant flow is at its normal winter rate and the blanket is at normal depth.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The ice cover has shrunk the effective basin area, channelling flow from inlet to outlet
Cold water has stopped the coagulant from working at all
The sludge blanket has frozen and is lifting into the effluent
The plant flow has risen beyond the clarifier rating

inference.explanation: Most of the surface is ice, flow is confined to a channel, dye crosses in 25 minutes, and floc settles well indoors. The ice has cut the effective settling area and created a channel. Coagulation still works per the cylinder test, flow is normal, and no blanket lifting is observed.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the ice channelling pattern?

options.label: Archived alum delivery records
Archived winter tracer and settled turbidity records from past cold snaps
Archived sludge blanket surveys

nextClue.explanation: Archived winter tracer and settled turbidity records from past cold snaps directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Alum deliveries were on schedule, and the cylinder test already shows the chemical works.
clueText.nc-b: Past winters show dye crossing in under 30 minutes whenever ice cover passed about half the surface, with normal times in open water.
clueText.nc-c: Blanket surveys through the winter stayed in the normal range.

tasks.prompt: The clarifier sludge blanket keeps rising even though the sludge pump runs continuously and sounds normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Sludge discharged at the pump outlet is thin and watery, with almost no solids, even with the pump running.
Suction pressure at the pump is abnormally high vacuum, and flow through the sludge line is a trickle.
Tapping along the sludge line finds a long section that sounds solid and does not vibrate with flow.
Blanket depth has risen steadily for four days and settled turbidity is beginning to suffer.
A spare pump connected to a different draw-off point pulls thick sludge normally.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge pump impeller is worn out
The sludge line is plugged, so the running pump cannot actually remove sludge
The clarifier is producing far more sludge than normal
The blanket depth gauge is reading falsely high

inference.explanation: Discharge is watery, suction vacuum is high with a trickle of flow, a line section sounds solid, and a spare pump on another draw-off pulls thick sludge. That is a plugged line. A worn impeller would not give high vacuum with a solid-sounding line, sludge production has no supporting observation, and the rising blanket is confirmed by the spare pump result.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms where this line plugs?

options.label: Archived pump curve test results
Archived raw-water solids loading records
Archived sludge line flushing and rodding maintenance history

nextClue.explanation: Archived sludge line flushing and rodding maintenance history directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: The pump curve test was satisfactory last quarter, and the pump pulls normally on the other draw-off point.
clueText.nc-b: Solids loading records are in their usual range for this season.
clueText.nc-c: History shows the same low elbow has plugged three times in five years, each time with high suction vacuum and watery discharge, and was cleared by rodding.

tasks.prompt: Settled turbidity is poor in the morning after cold nights, and a dye test shows a fast layer moving along the bottom of the clarifier.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: Raw water entering at dawn is 3 C colder and denser than the water stored in the basin overnight.
Dye released at the inlet dives and travels along the basin floor, reaching the outlet zone well ahead of the theoretical detention time.
Floc formed upstream is large and settles well in a cylinder test.
Surface water in the basin stays comparatively clear while turbidity is highest near the bottom outlet samples.
Flow, dose, and blanket depth are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The sludge blanket is being scoured off the floor by excessive flow
The coagulant dose falls overnight because the feed pump slows
A cold, dense inflow current is sliding under the basin contents and carrying floc toward the outlet
Warm water is rising through the basin and lifting the blanket

inference.explanation: The inflow is colder and denser, dye travels along the floor, and bottom samples are worst while the surface stays clearer. That is a density current. Flow is normal so floor scour is not supported, the dose is recorded normal, and a rising warm current would show the opposite temperature pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the density current pattern?

options.label: Archived basin temperature profiles and dye study notes from past cold nights
Archived sludge pump run log
Archived alum feed pump calibration sheet

nextClue.explanation: Archived basin temperature profiles and dye study notes from past cold nights directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Past profiles show the same cold bottom layer and early dye arrival whenever the dawn inflow ran at least 2 C colder than the basin.
clueText.nc-b: The sludge pump log is steady, which does not explain a bottom dye layer.
clueText.nc-c: The feed pump calibration was verified last week and dose records are flat overnight.

tasks.prompt: Floc leaving the flocculation basin is smaller and weaker than the floc seen in jar tests, and settled turbidity has risen since a basin speed change.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian Class 1 water plant log: steady plant flow unless noted, archived plant and laboratory records available for review.

evidence.label: The flocculator paddle speed was raised last week to what staff hoped would be a more vigorous setting.
Jar tests using gentle stirring after rapid mix form large floc that settles well at the plant dose.
Jar tests using vigorous stirring throughout break the floc into small fragments that settle poorly.
Floc size gets smaller along the basin, the opposite of normal growth toward the outlet.
Raw-water quality, dose, and pH are unchanged.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by the observations?

options.label: The alum dose is too low to form floc in the first place
The rapid mixer has failed and is not dispersing coagulant
Cold water is slowing floc growth
Excessive flocculator mixing is shearing floc apart after it forms

inference.explanation: Floc shrinks along the basin, gentle jar stirring works while vigorous jar stirring reproduces the damage, and the change followed a paddle speed increase. That is shear. A low dose or failed rapid mix would prevent formation in the gentle jar too, and no temperature drop is recorded.

nextClue.prompt: Which archived record best confirms the shear threshold?

options.label: Archived raw-water temperature log
Archived flocculator speed change log paired with settled turbidity trend
Archived alum delivery certificates

nextClue.explanation: Archived flocculator speed change log paired with settled turbidity trend directly records the condition behind the keyed explanation over time, so it best confirms it against the alternatives.

clueText.nc-a: Temperature held steady through the change, which removes cold water as the trigger.
clueText.nc-b: The trend shows settled turbidity rising the same day paddle speed was raised, and holding poor until speed was lowered in a brief trial.
clueText.nc-c: Delivery certificates show the alum met specification, matching the good gentle jar result.
